doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Trio with Jack Toker and Toker's meeting with Reggie Powell at Lou Rawls's show
summary: After Cavallo he formed a trio with drummer Jack Toker; Toker met Rawls's musical director Reg Powell in Seattle and was hired.

bands.name: Jimmy Cavallo and the House Rockers

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah, a little higher up. Talk about learning on the job, that’s great. Well okay and you did that for a while and you came back here. How do you get, how did the channels open up for you that eventually got you to the next level up?

Well after I left Jimmy Cavallo’s band, the bass player and I actually left together and formed a trio, and we picked up a drummer in Atlantic City where we were working, his name was Jack Toker, a wonderful drummer. And Jack and I and the bass player had a © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

group for about six months and that fell apart and I said okay, I decided I was going to come home, and the drummer said he was going to stay out on the road. Well he hooked up with a show band at that time, and this must have been ’69, ’70, right around that time. There were lots of gigs and so you could play the Holiday Inn circuit, you could keep working, again, covering songs on the radio, this stuff. So he got into a group that was pretty good about this, and they were all over the country. So he happened to land a gig in Seattle at a place called, I believe, the Trojan Horse was the name of it. And there were two rooms. There was a show room that had major acts, and then there was a smaller room which was a lounge, and that’s where they were playing, in this little lounge. So Lou Rawls had just come back from a European tour. He had lost his musical director so he picked up a guy in London named Reggie Powell, who had a degree from the Royal College of Music, he studied with Sir Richard Thomas Beecham, orchestration. He was a pretty cool guy. Plus he played great jazz piano and organ. So he became Lou’s musical director. Lou imported him into the U.S. Now not knowing anybody in the U.S., this guy, going into the lounge after a show, sees this band playing and having a drink, and my friend the drummer Jack Toker playing the gig. And he says “this guy’s pretty good.” So after their show he goes “hey, my name is Reg Powell and I’m in the other room there with Lou, and you know, I’d like to get your number because I like the way you play, and we may need a drummer sometime, you never know. I don’t know anybody in the States.” And Jack says “right.” So he gives him his phone number. And they became fast friends. I guess they were there for a month or something and they would jam in the afternoons, so they became fast friends musically and otherwise. So I get a phone call from Jack Toker and he says you’re never going to believe this, I’m gigging with Lou Rawls. Now at the time, Lou had just come off a hit called “A Natural Man” which everybody knew who he was, prior to that he had had jazz hits and so he was a jazz, blues, pop singer and working with him was a big deal. So I was very happy for him. So he said “look, we’re going to be in New York at the St. Regis Hotel. Why don’t you come down and put your guitar in the trunk. Come down and see the show and I’d like you to meet this piano player, you’re going to like him.” Okay fine. So I went down, I saw the show, met Lou Rawls, the first time I’d met a star. And the next afternoon we went down to the showroom which was closed, and the three of us played, piano, guitar and drums, and Reggie Powell says to me “hey, I like the way you play, why don’t you give me your phone number?” Déjà vu again. So that’s what happened. And a few months later we got called. Actually this is a side story that goes along with it. I was in another band, a local band, trying to get things going. And we had a trumpet player who was from New York. I’ll leave his name out, he might see this.
